rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at mid temperature to capture all 6 compounds without truncation and map the overall elution window. This run should reveal whether peaks are compressed early, late, or spread across the gradient so later injections can narrow the window and tune slope.

All pairs are already fully resolved, so the goal is to cut time by trimming the gradient to the observed elution window and making it steeper. The first and last peaks correspond to roughly phi_e about 0.18 and 0.68, so this narrower, shorter gradient should keep all peaks in-gradient while pulling the last peak closer to 10 min.

Resolution still has a large safety margin, so push for a shorter run by steepening the same well-targeted gradient and raising temperature one step to bring the last peak under 10 min. Keeping the window fixed isolates whether time can be reduced without sacrificing the currently generous worst-pair resolution.

A perfect CRF is already achieved, so now probe the speed limit by shortening the gradient one more step while holding the same selectivity settings. The current worst pair still has ample margin, so this test checks whether an even faster fully resolved method is possible before any pair drops below 1.5 or the last peak moves past 10 min.

Continue bracketing the minimum gradient time, since the 6 min method still has comfortable resolution and an 8.1 min last peak. This steeper run tests whether full resolution can be maintained at even shorter analysis time, with the early pair (1,2) now the likely limiting case.

The 4 min gradient still gives full-credit resolution with the worst pair at R=2.19, so the next step is to test the shortest allowed gradient on the same window. This should identify whether the method can be pushed to the minimum run time before the front pair loses resolution below 1.5.

At the 2 min limit the only failure is the front pair, suggesting the gradient is too strong at the start rather than too short overall. Lowering phi0 by one step should retain and spread the earliest two peaks more while keeping the run extremely fast and the later peaks still safely within the window.

The 2 min runs show the front pair is the limiting case and lowering phi0 did not help, so try temperature as the orthogonal lever while staying at the fastest gradient that previously gave full resolution. This checks whether a modest selectivity change can preserve or improve the critical pair while further shortening an already perfect method.

Higher temperature kept full resolution at 4 min and only modestly reduced the critical front-pair margin, so it is worth retesting the 2 min gradient under this new selectivity. This directly checks whether temperature can rescue the only failing fast method and deliver the shortest possible fully resolved run.

The limiting pair is always the first two peaks, so reduce the gradient range slightly at the high-phi end to make the slope shallower without delaying the early region much. This should test whether the 4 min method can gain front-pair margin while staying fully resolved and potentially still very fast.

Narrowing the window improved the critical front-pair margin at 4 min, so now test whether that gain is enough to make the 2 min gradient fully resolved. This is the most direct route to the shortest possible perfect method after the broader 2 min windows failed.

The 2 min, narrower-window method is close, and temperature clearly affects the limiting front pair; lowering T may restore selectivity enough to push R(1,2) over 1.5. This directly tests whether the shortest gradient can be rescued by the opposite temperature shift while keeping the same favorable slope.

The 2 min method is now just shy of full credit, so make the gradient slightly shallower by lowering phi1 one more step while keeping the same temperature that improved the critical pair. This should give the front pair the extra separation needed to cross R=1.5, while the last peak still has ample room under 10 min.

The 2 min, phi1 0.60 method at 40 C nearly reached full resolution with no time penalty, while reducing phi1 to 0.55 fixed resolution but pushed the last peak just beyond 10 min. Lowering temperature one more step at phi1 0.60 may provide the small selectivity gain needed for the front pair to reach R >= 1.5 while keeping the last peak under 10 min.

You already have a perfect 2 min method, so now test whether raising phi0 can trim the earliest retention and overall run time while preserving enough margin on the critical front pair. This is a focused optimization around the current fastest perfect condition without changing the successful slope or temperature.

Raising phi0 to 0.15 improved the critical pair and slightly accelerated the front end without hurting the last peak, so one more step up is a sensible boundary test. This probes whether the start can be made even stronger while still keeping the first pair above R=1.5 and maintaining the fastest perfect 2 min method.

The 2 min method remains perfect and the front pair continues to improve as phi0 increases, while the last peak is essentially unchanged. Testing phi0 at 0.25 explores whether the start can be made even more aggressive without pushing the first peak into the unretained region or losing the critical-pair margin.

The first peak is now very early, but still retained enough and all pairs remain fully resolved, so one more increase in phi0 can map the practical upper boundary. This tests whether further front-end acceleration is possible before the earliest peak becomes effectively unretained or the front pair starts to collapse.

At phi0 0.30 the first pair sits exactly at the full-credit boundary and the first peak is near the unretained region, so one final step up cleanly tests the limit. This should reveal whether 0.30 is the highest safe starting composition or whether a still stronger start remains viable.

Phi0 0.30 is the upper safe boundary, so now test whether raising phi1 can shorten the tail while keeping the front pair at or above the full-credit threshold. This exploits the fact that the late peak still dominates run length, whereas the front pair—not the tail—controls resolution.

The higher phi1 dramatically shortens the tail, and the only issue is the front pair sitting just below full credit at phi0 0.30. Dropping phi0 one step should restore a small amount of front-pair resolution while retaining most of the gain in last-peak time.

You now have a very fast perfect method, so test whether a further increase in phi1 can trim the last peak even more while the front pair still has healthy margin at R=1.80. This is the natural next boundary check because the late peak should respond strongly, whereas the front pair is the only likely failure mode.

The 2 min method remains perfect at phi1 0.70 with good margin on the front pair, and the last peak dropped substantially, so one more increase in phi1 is justified. This checks whether the tail can be compressed further before the front pair falls below the full-credit threshold.

Phi1 0.75 still gives a perfect score with the critical pair at R=1.59, so there is room for one more increase to probe the fastest viable endpoint. This should compress the tail further while showing whether the front pair remains above the 1.5 cutoff or if 0.75 is the true optimum boundary.

The current method is still perfect with the limiting pair exactly at R=1.50, so the final injection should test the next-higher phi1 boundary for an even faster fully resolved run. This is the highest-value remaining experiment because it can either establish a new fastest perfect method or confirm that phi1 0.80 is the optimum edge.
